episode.title: Sunlight Takes 8 Minutes to Reach Us
episode.central_question: What does the eight-minute delay of sunlight tell us about the universe and about life on Earth?

beats.name: Earth at scale
beats.because: Start with the size of home.

beats.name: The travel time
beats.because: Distance is easy to draw. Time is harder to feel.

beats.name: The Sun
beats.because: Now scale up: the Sun is far larger and far farther.

beats.name: The eight-minute gap
beats.because: Light is a clock. It shows us what happened in the past.

beats.name: Life on Earth
beats.because: Eight minutes is a fact about light. The bigger story is what sunlight does.

beats.name: The nearest other star
beats.because: Our Sun is not alone. The next star is much farther.

beats.name: The closing question
beats.because: Light always shows us a little of the past.

shots.voiceover: Right now, the sunlight on your face left the Sun about eight minutes ago.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

claims.text: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth

shots.voiceover: It crossed roughly 150 million kilometres of nearly empty space to reach you.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

claims.text: Sun-Earth distance about 150 million km (1 AU)

shots.voiceover: Nothing you see in daylight is happening in this exact moment.

visual.credit: NASA (JSC) / Karen Nyberg

shots.voiceover: It is all a little bit old.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Most of us never notice this, because light moves so fast that the delay is invisible.

visual.credit: NASA (JSC)

shots.voiceover: But it is there, every second of every day.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: In this episode we will follow that light from the Sun to Earth.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: We will ask what the delay really means for us.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Along the way, we will meet the Moon, the Sun, and the nearest star beyond them.

visual.credit: NASA (GSFC)

shots.voiceover: Start with home, the one place we all know.

visual.credit: NASA (GSFC) / NASA/GSFC/Bill Hrybyk

shots.voiceover: Earth is about 12,742 kilometres across, measured through its middle.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: That is a number we can picture, because we have all stood on its surface.

visual.credit: NASA (KSC) / NASA/Kim Shiflett

shots.voiceover: The Moon is much smaller, about a quarter of Earth's width.

visual.credit: NASA (JPL)

claims.text: Moon about a quarter of Earth's diameter

shots.voiceover: Yet it sits roughly thirty Earth-widths away, close enough to pull on our oceans and make the tides.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

claims.text: Moon about 30 Earth diameters away (384,400 km / 12,742 km, derived)

shots.voiceover: Picture thirty Earth-widths laid end to end between the two.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: That is the gap light must cross to reach the Moon.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: It is a long way for us, but a short trip for light.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Hold that picture in mind, because every distance in this episode is measured against it.

visual.credit: NASA (JPL)

shots.voiceover: Light is the fastest thing we know of; nothing carries information faster.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Even so, light needs time to cross space.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: To reach the Moon, it takes about one and a quarter seconds.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

claims.text: Light takes about 1.28 s to reach the Moon (384,400 km / c, derived)

shots.voiceover: That sounds quick, and it is.

visual.credit: NASA (JSC) / NASA

shots.voiceover: But distance turns into time, and time turns into a kind of delay.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: A signal sent to the Moon and back takes a few seconds.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: That is already enough to make a live conversation feel slightly off.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Engineers who control spacecraft on Mars plan around this delay, because their commands take minutes to arrive.

visual.credit: NASA (JPL)

shots.voiceover: The farther something is, the more out of date its light becomes.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Now the Sun, the star that sets our clock.

visual.credit: NASA (GSFC)

shots.voiceover: It is about 109 Earth diameters across.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Its distance from us is roughly 150 million kilometres.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

claims.text: Sun-Earth distance about 150 million km (1 AU)

shots.voiceover: Astronomers call that distance one astronomical unit, the standard yardstick of the solar system.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Real images of the Sun show its surface in fine detail.

visual.credit: NASA (JPL)

shots.voiceover: Dark sunspots, bright flares, and loops of glowing gas.

visual.credit: NASA (JPL)

shots.voiceover: They come from spacecraft that watch the Sun all the time.

visual.credit: NASA (KSC) / NASA/Kim Shiflett

shots.voiceover: Put the size and the distance together, and you get the central number of this episode.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Sunlight needs about eight minutes and twenty seconds to cover that gap.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

claims.text: Sunlight takes about 8 min 20 s to reach Earth

shots.voiceover: Every image of the Sun you have ever seen is a snapshot of a few minutes ago.

visual.credit: NASA (JPL)

shots.voiceover: Inside the Sun, energy from nuclear fusion starts its journey.

visual.credit: NASA (JPL)

shots.voiceover: It takes a very long time to escape as light.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Follow that light for a moment.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: It leaves the Sun's surface, crosses empty space, and slips into Earth's atmosphere.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: It moves at roughly 300,000 kilometres every second.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

claims.text: Light travels about 300,000 km per second

shots.voiceover: Now imagine the Sun switched off this very second.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: You would not notice anything for eight minutes.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: The sky would look normal, the warmth on your skin would feel the same.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: The light would keep arriving as if nothing had happened.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Only after those minutes would it stop.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Physics also says the Sun's gravity would take about the same time to change.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

claims.text: Sun's gravity change would take about the same time as its light; theoretical prediction

shots.voiceover: That is a prediction we cannot test directly.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: What is certain is this: light always tells you the past, never the present.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Astronomers use the same idea to study the past.

visual.credit: NASA (GSFC)

shots.voiceover: When you look at a distant galaxy, you are seeing it as it was long ago.

visual.credit: NASA (GSFC)

shots.voiceover: Eight minutes of delay is a fact about light.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: The bigger story is what sunlight does once it arrives.

visual.credit: NASA (JSC)

shots.voiceover: Almost every food chain on our planet starts with it.

visual.credit: NASA (JPL)

claims.text: Almost every food chain starts with sunlight

shots.voiceover: Plants, algae and some bacteria capture that energy and turn it into food.

visual.credit: NASA (GSFC)

shots.voiceover: Animals eat them, and other animals eat those animals.

visual.credit: NASA (KSC) / NASA/Glenn Benson

shots.voiceover: Seasons, weather and the water cycle are all driven by the energy that arrives in those eight minutes.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Sunlight also warms the ocean surface.

visual.credit: NASA (JSC)

shots.voiceover: That warmth drives currents that move heat around the planet.

visual.credit: NASA (JSC)

shots.voiceover: Yet there is an exception.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Deep in the ocean, far below the reach of sunlight, there are hydrothermal vents.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: They release hot, chemical-rich water from Earth's interior.

visual.search_query: NOAA black smoker vent, real photo
visual.credit: NOAA Office of Ocean Exploration and Research

claims.text: Hydrothermal vents release hot, chemical-rich water

shots.voiceover: Microbes there turn those chemicals into energy.

visual.credit: IFE, URI-IAO, UW, Lost City Science Party; NOAA/OAR/OER; The Lost City 2005 Expedition

shots.voiceover: Life does not strictly need the Sun, even though most life on Earth depends on it.

visual.search_query: Tube worms at a vent, real photo
visual.credit: OAR/National Undersea Research Program (NURP)

shots.voiceover: Our Sun is the nearest star to Earth, but it is not alone.

visual.credit: NASA (JPL)

shots.voiceover: The next nearest star is Proxima Centauri.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Its light takes about four years to reach us.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

claims.text: Proxima Centauri light takes about 4.24 years to reach Earth

shots.voiceover: Proxima Centauri is part of a three-star system, with Alpha Centauri A and B nearby.

visual.credit: NASA (GSFC)

shots.voiceover: That light set out before anyone on Earth could see it, and it has been travelling ever since.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Compare that with our own Sun, whose light needs eight minutes.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Proxima Centauri is a small, faint red star.

visual.credit: NASA (JPL)

shots.voiceover: It is too dim to see with the naked eye from most places.

visual.credit: NASA (JPL)

shots.voiceover: Yet it follows the same rule.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Every star you see is a message that left it long ago.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: The farther the star, the older the message.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: So here is the question.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: Every sunrise you have ever watched was eight minutes old by the time it reached your eyes.

visual.credit: NASA (JSC)

claims.text: Sunrise light is about eight minutes old when it reaches us

shots.voiceover: Every star you have ever seen is older than your sense of time.

visual.credit: NASA (JPL)

shots.voiceover: Light lets us see the universe, but it always shows us a little of the past.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: The next time you stand in sunlight, notice the warmth on your skin.

visual.credit: NASA (JSC)

shots.voiceover: Remember where it came from.

visual.credit: NASA (JSC)

shots.voiceover: It left the Sun eight minutes ago.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: It crossed the emptiness between us and arrived in time for you to feel it.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Earth, Moon and Sun maps from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

shots.voiceover: So what else in your sky is already old?

visual.credit: NASA (JSC)
